title: Apple and cinnamon fruit leather
subtitle: pureed apple spread thin and dried to a chewy, pliable sheet
excerpt: Apple and cinnamon fruit leather is a smooth apple puree spread thin on a lined baking tray and dried in a very low oven for several hours until it sets to a chewy, pliable sheet. The natural sugar in cooked apple is enough that only a little added sugar is needed. The sheet peels cleanly from the paper once fully dry and can be rolled or cut into strips.
sourceNotes: Fruit leather is a traditional form of fruit preservation documented in British and American preserving books from the nineteenth century onward. The oven-drying method is the modern home adaptation of sun-drying.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps rolled in baking paper at room temperature for up to 2 weeks, or in the fridge for up to 1 month.
recipe.temperatureNote: 70 degrees C (fan 50 degrees C / gas at the lowest setting) for drying

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: 70 degrees C (fan 50 degrees C / very low gas)

content.text: Apple and cinnamon fruit leather is pureed apple spread thin on a lined baking tray and dried in a very low oven until it is pliable and no longer sticky. Cooking the apples first concentrates the flavour and makes the puree smooth enough to spread evenly. The sheet peels away cleanly from the paper once fully dry.

items.prepNote: about 4 medium apples, peeled, cored, and chopped

content.text: Put the chopped apple, sugar, cinnamon, and water into a medium saucepan. Cook over a medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, for 12 to 15 minutes until the apples are completely soft and falling apart.

Blend until completely smooth, either in a food processor or with a stick blender. Taste and add a little more sugar or cinnamon if needed. The puree should taste slightly more intense than you want the finished leather to taste, as it will concentrate further during drying.

Heat the oven to 70 degrees C (fan 50 degrees C, or gas on its very lowest setting). Line a large baking tray with a silicone mat or baking paper. Pour the puree onto the tray and spread it to a thin, even layer about 3 mm deep with a spatula. Aim for the same depth all over, as thin patches dry faster and thick patches stay sticky.

Place in the oven and dry for 4 to 6 hours, checking every hour from hour 3. The leather is done when the surface is no longer sticky to the touch and peels away cleanly from the paper without tearing.
Remove from the oven and leave to cool for 10 minutes on the tray. Peel the sheet off the paper and lay it on a fresh sheet of baking paper. Cut into strips or roll up in the paper for storage.

attrs.problem: Leather sticky after the full drying time
attrs.avoid: Avoid high oven temperatures; the outside dries and seals before the moisture can escape from beneath.
attrs.fix: Return to the oven on the lowest possible setting for another hour. If the oven does not go below 100 degrees C, leave the door slightly ajar to reduce the temperature.

attrs.problem: Leather cracking and brittle rather than pliable
attrs.avoid: Avoid over-drying; leather that has lost too much moisture becomes brittle and breaks on folding.
attrs.fix: Remove from the oven a little earlier. The leather should feel dry on the surface but still pliable and slightly soft in the centre.

attrs.problem: Leather sticking to the paper on the tray
attrs.avoid: Avoid plain baking paper without any fat; the puree bonds to it as it dries.
attrs.fix: Use a silicone baking mat, which releases cleanly, or lightly oil the baking paper before pouring on the puree.
